title: The Creator Economy Vision Behind 8 Circuit Studios
content: Michael co-founded 8 Circuit Studios with a vision to democratize game development using blockchain technology. His core insight was that traditional game development concentrated profits with large publishers while the developers, designers, and artists doing the actual work were underpaid and overworked. He envisioned a system where game assets — characters, environments, items, rifles, etc. — would be tokenized on the blockchain with standardized protocols enabling them to move between games and environments. Original creators of those assets would receive a residual payment every time their work was used, functioning like a creator economy for game assets. This was designed to build the infrastructure layer for the Metaverse before the term was commercialized by Facebook. The company first shipped a proof-of-concept NFT game called Alien Arsenal (pivoted to after observing CryptoKitties' success), then focused on the primary title Project Genesis, which is still available on Steam today. Michael's co-founder ultimately wanted to focus on building the game rather than building the Web3 infrastructure, and as the Web3 space developed a negative reputation due to bad actors, Michael decided to part ways. His co-founder continues developing Project Genesis.

title: Building Web3 Infrastructure Without a Playbook
content: During his three years at 8 Circuit Studios, Michael spent most of his time architecting the Web3 backend: designing how digital assets would be managed, how they would move between games, and what protocols would govern cross-game interoperability. A major challenge was the absence of Layer 2 blockchain solutions at the time, which meant the team had to build foundational infrastructure from scratch rather than relying on existing tools. This experience forced Michael to develop the ability to solve novel problems without reference material or established solutions — a capability he identifies as one of the most valuable skills he developed during that period.

title: Diagnosing a CEO as the Hidden Root Cause of Stalled Product Delivery

question: What's the most common problem you find when you start working with a new client?
answer: The most common issue is poorly defined handoffs between teams. Teams don't have a shared definition of what 'done' means when passing work from one group to another — whether that's art to design, design to development, or development to QA. The result is delays, missing documentation, miscommunication, excess meetings, and Slack threads that exist only because the right information wasn't included in the original handoff. The fix sounds simple, but most organizations don't recognize it as the root cause of their larger operational problems. Defining clear handoff criteria and required deliverables at each transition point removes an enormous amount of ongoing friction.

title: How Michael Built Distills: From Personal AI Workflow Problem to Product
content: Distills originated from a personal workflow problem Michael encountered while working across multiple LLMs simultaneously — primarily Claude, ChatGPT, and a locally hosted LLM he built himself. Each session required re-establishing context, and there was no shared memory layer across systems: Claude had no persistent memory at the time, ChatGPT's memory was internal and unexposed, and his local LLM had limited memory capability. To solve this, Michael built a system in which any LLM he worked with would output structured data in JSON format. A local LLM acted as a JSON ledger manager, consolidating information from all sessions into a single accessible location. Any LLM could then load relevant project context from that ledger on demand. Michael also maintained memory files for every project he worked on, documenting decisions made, implementation details, reasoning behind choices, and steps taken — typically outputted as case studies. Recognizing that he had rich documentation about his career and projects that wasn't surfaceable through a standard portfolio site, he built a JavaScript RAG widget and chatbot to make it queryable. He then used a chatbot interview process to fill in narrative gaps and clarify details. The result became Distills, a product he is preparing for public release.

Michael's primary target user for Distills is job seekers. He sees it as a tool to help candidates get past the first round of screening by giving recruiters a way to interact with a knowledge base about the candidate — replacing or supplementing early recruiter calls. title: How a Player Death Visualization Tool Became the Halo Kill Cam
content: Situation: Michael was the lead SDET at Microsoft working with third-party studio Hired Gun on an Xbox 360 title called Voodoo Vents. User testing revealed a level approximately 45–60 minutes into gameplay that no test players could complete. The developer's designers — who played the game daily — pushed back repeatedly, insisting the difficulty was intentional. What Michael did: Rather than continuing to report findings verbally, he and an engineer instrumented the game's codebase to log player deaths — including time of death, location, and game state. They loaded the aggregated data into the game itself and used the fly-around camera mode to display colored boxes at each player's death location. Flying through the problematic level made it immediately visible which specific locations were causing deaths. Outcome: The designers saw the data and immediately agreed to fix the specific problem areas. The tool spread to other Microsoft game teams, was added to the Xbox SDK, and a patent was filed. The Bungie team building Halo adopted the tool and evolved it into the kill shot replay cam — one of the most beloved features in the franchise.

question: What is the story behind Michael's patent that led to the Halo kill cam?
answer: While serving as lead SDET at Microsoft on an Xbox 360 title called Voodoo Vents (developed by third-party studio Hired Gun), Michael needed to prove to resistant developers that a specific level was too difficult. He and an engineer instrumented the game's code to log player deaths with location and timing data, loaded that data into the game, and used the fly-around camera to display colored markers at each death location. The visualization made the problem undeniable. The tool spread across Microsoft's game teams, was added to the Xbox SDK, and a patent was filed. Bungie adopted the tool for Halo and evolved it into the kill shot replay cam.

content: After the death-visualization tool was successful, Michael extended it to support in-the-moment player feedback. title: Transforming Kabam's Release Process from Chaos to Repeatability

He added a beta test team for new features, a play test team for ongoing balance checks, and an automation team for build automation. He also created a test environment (previously only dev and production existed) and set up a CDN traffic-switching system: builds were pushed to the test environment, tested, and then the CDN was switched to point at the former test environment as the new live environment, with zero downtime. He also introduced agile development practices across the organization. These changes transformed an unpredictable release cadence into a repeatable, quality-controlled process.

title: Getting a Resistant Engineering Lead to Embrace Project Planning at Kinoo
content: At Kinoo, Michael was the first non-founder hire and was responsible for pulling a 120-person cross-functional team together to ship a complex AR gaming and communication platform on a nine-month timeline set by the CEO and board. Michael tried Jira (rejected), then several other tools (none stuck), and finally created a Miro board with a spreadsheet overlay and rough estimates. The engineer became angry because the estimates were inaccurate. Michael responded: 'Then sit down with me and let's talk through what's right.' The turning point came when Michael pointed out that the design team was missing the engineer's handoff deadlines because they didn't know when he needed deliverables — a direct consequence of having no schedule. This made the cost of not planning concrete and immediate. The engineer began engaging with scheduling to protect his own team's workflow. Within three to four months, the same engineer was proactively saying 'let's go look at the schedule' whenever new work came up. Michael had migrated the planning from Miro to Smartsheet by that point.

title: Converting a Resistant Lead Engineer into a Planning Champion at Kinoo
content: Situation: At Kinoo, Michael was leading a 120-person cross-functional program on an AR platform. The company skipped the planning phase after prototyping. The head of software engineering refused to engage with Jira or any formal planning, felt overwhelmed by coding demands, and became angry at dependent teams when they couldn't deliver what he needed — even though he hadn't shared his plans with them. The CEO told Michael to back off. What Michael did: Michael created a visual schedule in Miro (a tool the engineer already used) with large blocks representing estimated tasks. He intentionally presented it as his own rough guess and invited the engineer to correct it. The engineer pushed back — which led to daily 1–2 hour working sessions for about a week to collaboratively build out the real schedule. Michael then used that schedule to synchronize the design team's delivery timeline. When the engineer began moving blocks around at night without notifying anyone, Michael migrated the planning system to Smartsheet, which integrated with Jira for ticket creation. Outcome: Within 3–4 months, the engineer who had refused all planning became the first person to say 'let's go look at the schedule' when new tasks or changes were proposed. He became a champion of the planning process he had previously resisted.

title: Phase One of Michael's Three-Tier AI-Augmented PMO Framework

title: How Michael's Xbox Gameplay Instrumentation Patent Came to Be
content: While working on the Voodoo Vents platformer at Microsoft, Michael faced a persistent problem: external level designers refused to accept verbal feedback that their levels were too difficult. One level, approximately 30–40 minutes into the game and designed like Frogger, was so hard that every playtester had to be manually skipped past it. One player died over 100 times on that single level. To make the problem impossible to ignore, Michael collaborated with an on-site developer to instrument the entire game: every button press, death, item collection, and player action was written to a local log with a timestamp and in-game coordinates. The team then parsed all playtester logs, loaded the aggregate data onto an Xbox dev kit, and built a fly-through visualization that displayed every death location as geometry — stacks of boxes showing exactly where players were failing. This made the problem spatially undeniable to the designers. They changed the level layouts, and the instrumentation tool was used throughout the rest of development to pinpoint specific difficulty spikes rather than making wholesale difficulty reductions. Michael then pitched the system to other game teams across Microsoft. The Halo team adopted and extended the approach, using similar log data to generate in-game kill replays for multiplayer — the feature millions of players know as the kill cam. The work was filed as a patent with Microsoft's legal team; Michael is listed as inventor along with the developer who built it and several contributors. The patent eventually became part of the Xbox SDK, making the capability available to all developers on the platform.

title: What is Distills?
content: Distills is an AI-powered professional identity platform. Professionals upload career documents, complete a guided AI interview, and receive a hosted chatbot profile at distills.app/c/<slug>. Visitors to the profile can chat with the AI to learn about the person's background, skills, and experience — any time, without the professional needing to be present.

title: Core value proposition
content: Distills turns your career history into a conversational AI that represents you. Instead of a static resume or a LinkedIn profile that no one reads carefully, you get an interactive profile where anyone — a recruiter, a client, a collaborator — can ask specific questions and get detailed, accurate answers drawn from your actual documents and interview.

title: Step 1 — Upload documents
content: The first step is uploading your career documents: resume, portfolio, case studies, project write-ups, anything that captures your work. Supported formats include PDF, DOCX, and plain text. This takes about 5 minutes. The AI extracts structured knowledge from your files to build an initial knowledge base.

title: Step 2 — AI interview
content: After uploading, you complete a guided AI interview. The AI asks you questions about your experience, projects, skills, values, and work style — drilling into specifics that documents often miss. The interview typically takes 20 to 30 minutes. Your answers are transcribed and merged with the document knowledge to create a richer, more nuanced knowledge base.

title: Step 3 — Live profile instantly
content: Once the interview is complete, your knowledge base is compiled and your profile goes live immediately at distills.app/c/your-slug. Visitors arrive at a clean, professional page and can start chatting with your AI right away. No waiting, no approval process.

question: How long does setup take?
answer: The full setup — uploading documents and completing the AI interview — takes about 30 to 45 minutes for most people. Document upload is around 5 minutes, and the interview itself runs 20 to 30 minutes depending on how much detail you share. Once you submit, your live profile is available immediately.

title: Pricing overview
content: Distills has three tiers: Free, Pro, and Studio. Free gives you the full interview and a downloadable knowledge base. Pro ($24/month or $199/year) adds a hosted profile page at distills.app, analytics, photo and bio, and a custom slug. Studio ($49/month or $399/year) is designed for multiple chatbots and agency use.

question: What does the free tier include?
answer: The free tier runs the full AI interview and builds your complete knowledge base — no limits there. You get a downloadable knowledge.jsonl file and an embeddable chatbot widget you can add to any website with a single script tag. What the free tier does NOT include is a hosted profile at distills.app — for that you need Pro or Studio. There is a "Built with Distills" attribution requirement on self-hosted free widgets.

question: How much does Pro cost?
answer: Pro is $24 per month, or $199 per year (which works out to about $16.58/month — a 30% saving). Pro includes everything in Free plus: a hosted profile at distills.app/c/your-slug, profile analytics showing who visited and what they asked, a profile photo and bio, a custom URL slug, and the ability to enrich your knowledge base with additional content.

question: How much does Studio cost?
answer: Studio is $49 per month, or $399 per year. It is designed for professionals who need multiple chatbot profiles — for example, consultants who want separate profiles for different service lines, or agencies building profiles for clients. It includes all Pro features plus support for multiple chatbots under one account.

content: Annual billing saves 30% compared to monthly. Pro annual is $199/year ($16.58/month effective). Studio annual is $399/year ($33.25/month effective). No credit card is required to start with the free tier.

question: Who is Distills for?
answer: Distills is built for professionals who want an interactive way to share their expertise. The primary users are: freelancers and consultants who pitch to clients and want a smarter way to answer "what do you do?"; job seekers who want to supplement their resume with a richer, conversational profile; coaches and advisors who field the same questions from prospects over and over; and speakers or thought leaders who want a deeper way for audiences to engage with their work and ideas.

title: Target users and use cases
content: The main use cases for Distills are: (1) Job search — add your profile link to your email signature, resume footer, or LinkedIn so recruiters can ask detailed questions 24/7. (2) Client pitching — freelancers and consultants share the link with prospects before discovery calls. (3) Thought leadership — authors, coaches, and speakers let audiences explore their ideas conversationally. (4) Self-hosting — developers and technical users who prefer to run the chatbot on their own site use the free tier's downloadable widget.

question: How is Distills different from a LinkedIn profile?
answer: LinkedIn is a read-only social network. Visitors scroll a static page and must figure out what is relevant to them. Distills is conversational — visitors ask specific questions and get specific answers drawn from your actual experience. A recruiter can ask "Have you managed a team through a platform migration?" and your AI will answer with real detail from your documents and interview. LinkedIn also requires you to maintain an account there; Distills is your own hosted page. The two complement each other: use LinkedIn for discovery and networking, use your Distills profile for depth.

title: Distills vs. a traditional resume
content: A resume is a two-page summary constrained by format and space. A Distills profile has no length limit — the AI can speak to any aspect of your career in detail. Resumes are also passive: the reader extracts what they want. Distills is active: the AI surfaces exactly what each visitor needs. Your resume gets you an interview; your Distills profile wins the conversation before the interview even happens.

title: How the AI interview works
content: The AI interview is a guided conversation where Claude asks you structured questions about your professional background. It covers your career timeline, key projects, skills, tools, work style, values, and how you approach challenges. The AI reads your uploaded documents first and then asks follow-up questions to fill gaps and capture nuance that documents miss. All answers are captured, processed, and merged into your knowledge base.

question: Can I skip the interview and just use my documents?
answer: You must complete at least the basic interview to generate a profile. The interview is how Distills captures context that documents miss — your reasoning, values, work style, and specifics about your projects. That said, you can move through the interview quickly; there is no minimum answer length. The more detail you share, the better your chatbot performs.

title: What the hosted profile looks like
content: Your hosted profile at distills.app/c/your-slug is a clean, professional single-page app. It shows your name, photo (Pro), bio (Pro), and a chat interface. Visitors type questions and get streaming AI responses in real time. There are no ads, no distractions, and no Distills branding beyond a small footer attribution on free profiles. The page is mobile-responsive and works in all modern browsers.

question: What is the URL for my profile?
answer: Free tier profiles do not get a hosted URL — they are self-hosted only. Pro and Studio profiles are hosted at distills.app/c/your-slug. On Pro, you can choose a custom slug (e.g., distills.app/c/jane-smith). The slug must be unique across all Distills profiles. You can share this URL in your email signature, on LinkedIn, in your resume, or anywhere else.

title: Pro tier features
content: Pro includes everything in Free plus: hosted profile at distills.app, profile photo and bio displayed on the page, custom URL slug, analytics dashboard showing daily views and questions, topic breakdown of what visitors are asking, question gap detection (what visitors asked that the AI could not answer well), knowledge base enrichment (adding new content without re-running the interview), and resume download button on the profile.

question: What analytics does Pro include?
answer: Pro analytics show: daily view and question counts over the last 30 days, total monthly queries, a topic breakdown showing what subjects visitors ask about most, and a knowledge gap report listing questions visitors asked that the AI could not answer confidently. This data helps you understand who is visiting your profile and what they need.

title: AI model used for chat
content: Profile chat is powered by Claude (claude-haiku-4-5) from Anthropic. The interview and knowledge base building use Claude Sonnet. The RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) system retrieves the most relevant knowledge base entries for each visitor question and passes them to Claude as context, ensuring answers are grounded in your actual information rather than generated from training data.

question: Does the AI make things up?
answer: The chat AI is instructed to answer only from your knowledge base and to say it does not know if the information is not there. It is grounded by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which means it can only cite what is in your knowledge base. It will not infer or fabricate details. If a visitor asks something not covered, the AI says so honestly rather than guessing.

question: What happens to my uploaded documents?
answer: Your uploaded files are processed to extract structured knowledge entries. Documents are stored in secure cloud storage (Cloudflare R2) and are not used to train AI models. The knowledge extracted from your documents lives in your knowledge base, which you can download as a knowledge.jsonl file at any time. You retain ownership of your data.

content: Distills does not collect personal data from profile visitors beyond what is needed for rate limiting (IP addresses). Visitor questions are logged for your analytics dashboard but are not sold or shared. No cookies are set on visitor profiles. Distills is built on Cloudflare's global edge network.

Each Distills profile chatbot has a daily question quota: 20 questions per day per profile, and 5 questions per day per individual visitor IP. These limits reset at midnight UTC. If a profile reaches its daily limit, visitors see a message to check back tomorrow. The limits exist to keep the service affordable while preventing abuse.

question: Do I need technical skills to use Distills?
answer: No. The hosted tiers (Pro and Studio) require no technical skill at all. You upload documents through a web interface, answer interview questions in a chat UI, and get a live profile URL. The free tier, if you choose to self-host the chatbot widget, requires pasting a script tag into your website's HTML — which is a 5-minute task for most developers or platforms like Webflow.

question: Can I update my chatbot later?
answer: Yes. You can re-run the wizard at any time to generate a fresh knowledge base from new documents and a new interview. Pro users can also enrich their existing knowledge base with new content without re-running the full interview. A direct editing dashboard for modifying individual knowledge entries without re-running the interview is on the roadmap.

title: Self-hosting the free chatbot widget
content: Free tier users receive a chatbot-widget.js file they can add to any website with a single script tag. The widget connects to the Distills API using the knowledge.jsonl from their account. Self-hosted widgets require "Built with Distills" attribution. This option is popular with developers who prefer to control hosting and branding entirely.

question: How does Distills compare to a personal website?
answer: A personal website requires ongoing maintenance — writing content, updating pages, managing hosting and domain. Distills is almost zero-maintenance: you set it up once and the AI handles all visitor questions from there. Distills also provides depth that a website cannot: the AI can answer any specific question a visitor has, not just what you chose to write about. That said, the two complement each other — link to your Distills profile from your website's contact or about page.

question: How is this different from just using ChatGPT or Claude directly?
answer: General AI chatbots like ChatGPT have no knowledge of your specific career. They would answer questions about you with generic information or simply admit they do not know. Distills builds a custom knowledge base from your actual documents and interview, so the AI answers specifically and accurately about you — your projects, your experience, your approach. It is the difference between a generic assistant and one trained on your professional history.

content: Distills currently supports English only. The interview and knowledge extraction are designed and tuned for English-language documents and responses. Multi-language support is on the roadmap. The daily chat quota is 20 questions per profile per day. Documents must be in PDF, DOCX, or plain text format.

question: How do I get started with Distills?
answer: Visit distills.app and click "Get started free" or "Create your AI profile." title: What to prepare before starting
content: Before running the Distills wizard, gather your career documents: resume (required), LinkedIn profile export (optional), portfolio pieces, case studies, project write-ups, bio, or any other professional writing that captures your work. The more material you provide, the richer your knowledge base. You can always add more documents by running the wizard again.

question: Can I cancel my subscription?
answer: Yes. You can cancel Pro or Studio at any time from your dashboard. Cancellation takes effect at the end of your current billing period. After cancellation, your profile moves to free tier — it will no longer be publicly hosted at distills.app, but you retain your knowledge base and can re-activate at any time.

content: Payments are processed by Stripe. Distills does not store credit card information. Stripe supports all major credit cards and debit cards. Billing is in USD. Annual plans are billed as a single upfront payment (one payment of $199 for Pro, $399 for Studio).

title: How professionals share their Distills profile
content: Common ways professionals share their Distills profile URL: adding it to their email signature, including it as a link in their resume ("Chat with my AI: distills.app/c/jane-smith"), adding it to their LinkedIn "Website" field, including it in a cover letter, sharing it with clients before discovery calls, and putting it in a speaker bio or conference program. The URL is permanent and shareable anywhere.

title: Infrastructure and reliability
content: Distills is built entirely on Cloudflare's global edge network. The backend runs as Cloudflare Workers (serverless), which means zero cold starts and sub-100ms response times globally. Storage uses Cloudflare R2 (documents and knowledge bases) and Cloudflare D1 (account and session database). This infrastructure gives Distills 99.9%+ uptime without the complexity of managing servers.

question: Is Distills free to try?

The only thing the free tier does not include is a hosted profile at distills.app — for that you upgrade to Pro. So you can experience everything Distills does before paying anything.

question: Can visitors chat anonymously with my profile?
